rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 (Materials and methods; Results) - the authors report their own greenhouse experiment inoculating 60 cucumber seedlings, collecting daily chlorophyll fluorescence images over 10 days, and training an improved ResNet50 model (Table 3, Figs 16-18).
rows.notes: The study only shows early detection/classification of cucumber downy mildew in seedlings (94.76% accuracy, detection ~3-4 days before visible symptoms) using a FluorCam chlorophyll fluorescence imaging system at 40 cm from the leaf in a greenhouse. It does not apply pesticides, does not target treatment to afflicted areas, and does not measure any reduction in chemical use or environmental effect; the Discussion only speculates that the approach 'may be more effective and cost-efficient in preventing the spread' than removing infected parts. Thus it supports at most a precondition (detection) of the claimed effect (targeted pesticide application reducing chemical consumption). Additionally, the technology is proximal leaf-level fluorescence imaging in a greenhouse rather than remote-sensing field maps of disease spatial distribution, so a technology mismatch is also flagged.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Study is a single-site greenhouse experiment on one cucumber cultivar; authors note limitations of inference speed and field/large-greenhouse applicability, but these concern detection, not the claimed pest-control effect.
